# Create an interactive drag-to-rotate ggcube

Creates an interactive HTML widget that you can rotate by dragging.
Pre-renders a set of ggcube plots across a 1D or 2D grid of rotation
angles and packages them as an htmlwidgets widget. The widget displays
in the RStudio Viewer, embeds in R Markdown and Quarto documents, works
in Shiny (see
[`orbit3dOutput()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/orbit_3d-shiny.md)),
and can be written to a self-contained HTML file with `file =`. When
viewing it, navigate through the views by dragging the image or using
the keyboard arrows.

## Usage

``` r
orbit_3d(
  plot,
  pitch = NULL,
  roll = NULL,
  yaw = NULL,
  light_azimuth = NULL,
  light_elevation = NULL,
  n = 36,
  loop = NULL,
  start = NULL,
  max_frames = 500,
  width = 480,
  height = 480,
  res = 96,
  cores = 1,
  device = "png",
  progress = interactive(),
  file = NULL,
  readout = FALSE
)
```

## Arguments

- plot:

  A ggplot object that uses
  [`coord_3d()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/coord_3d.md).

- pitch, roll, yaw:

  Rotation angles in degrees. Each is either a single value (held fixed)
  or a length-2 range `c(from, to)` that becomes a draggable axis. For
  `yaw`, using a larger value for `from` than `to` gives more natural
  results. Values specified here replace the ones specified in
  [`coord_3d()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/coord_3d.md).
  See Details.

- light_azimuth, light_elevation:

  Light direction in degrees, using the same conventions as
  [`direction()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/direction.md):
  azimuth is a bearing clockwise from the positive y axis, and elevation
  is the angle above the xy plane (between -90 and 90). Each is either a
  single value (held fixed) or a length-2 range `c(from, to)` that
  becomes a draggable axis. When either is given, the other is held at
  the plot light's current value unless also given; when both are `NULL`
  (the default), lighting is left as the plot specifies. These move the
  plot-level light set with
  [`light()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/light.md)
  or `coord_3d(light = )`, which must be directional (not
  `position`-based); it is an error to use them when lighting is
  disabled or when any layer has its own `light`. The light's `anchor`
  is respected: with the default `anchor = "scene"` the light moves
  around the data, so orbiting `yaw` and `light_azimuth` together partly
  cancels out; with `anchor = "camera"` it moves around the viewer.

- n:

  Grid resolution. For a 1D orbit, a single number giving the frame
  count. For a 2D orbit, a length-2 vector giving the counts for the
  horizontal and vertical screen axes respectively (in that order, x
  then y). Its length must match the number of ranged parameters.
  Default is 36.

- loop:

  Controls seamless wraparound. `NULL` (default) auto-detects looping
  independently for each axis by checking whether that axis returns to
  its starting view. `TRUE` or `FALSE` force wrapping on or off for all
  axes.

- start:

  Initial viewing angle(s) the orbit opens at, given in degrees as a
  named vector matching the variable axes, e.g. `start = c(yaw = 30)`,
  `start = c(yaw = 30, roll = 45)`, or `start = c(light_azimuth = 90)`.
  For a 1D orbit a bare scalar (e.g. `start = 30`) is also accepted. The
  orbit opens at the frame nearest each given angle. Any variable axis
  not named in `start` opens at the midpoint of its range, as does every
  axis when `start = NULL` (the default). Naming an axis that is fixed
  rather than variable throws an error.

- max_frames:

  Safety cap on the total number of rendered frames (`prod(n)`). A 2D
  grid can become very large; if the requested grid exceeds this cap the
  function errors rather than rendering. Raise it to allow larger grids.
  Default is 500.

- width, height:

  Dimensions of the animation in pixels. Defaults to 480 x 480.

- res:

  Resolution in ppi for the rendered frames. Default is 96. Controls the
  size of point-based text/lines/point elements relative to the plot.
  See [`?grDevices::png`](https://rdrr.io/r/grDevices/png.html) for
  details.

- cores:

  Number of CPU cores for parallel frame rendering. Default is 1
  (sequential). Values greater than 1 use
  [`parallel::parLapply()`](https://rdrr.io/r/parallel/clusterApply.html)
  to render frames in parallel, which can significantly speed up
  animation of complex plots. Note that progress reporting is not
  available during parallel rendering.

- device:

  The graphics device to use for rendering frames. Default is `"png"`.
  Other options include `"ragg_png"` (requires the ragg package).

- progress:

  Whether to print a progress bar. Ignored when `cores > 1`.

- file:

  Optional path to write a self-contained HTML file (via
  [`htmlwidgets::saveWidget()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/htmlwidgets/man/saveWidget.html)).
  If `NULL` (default), no file is written and the widget is simply
  returned for display or embedding.

- readout:

  Logical. Whether the orbit opens with a readout in its corner showing
  the angles of the current view, which you can copy into
  [`coord_3d()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/coord_3d.md)
  to reproduce it. The readout always lists `pitch`, `roll`, and `yaw`,
  and adds the light's azimuth and elevation (for use with
  [`direction()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/direction.md))
  when the orbit moves the light. Angles are shown in the terms you gave
  them: an orbit over `yaw = c(0, 360)` reports values from 0 to 360.
  This sets only how the orbit opens: pressing `r` while the orbit has
  focus shows or hides the readout either way. Default is `FALSE`.

## Value

A `orbit_3d` htmlwidget. Printed at the console it opens in the RStudio
Viewer or browser; in a knitr document it embeds automatically; in Shiny
use
[`orbit3dOutput()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/orbit_3d-shiny.md)
and
[`renderOrbit3d()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/orbit_3d-shiny.md).

## Specifying rotation and lighting

Each of `pitch`, `roll`, `yaw`, `light_azimuth`, and `light_elevation`
is given either as a single value (held fixed) or as a length-2 range
`c(from, to)` that is a variable, draggable axis. The number of ranges
determines the interaction:

- One range gives a 1D orbit: horizontal drag (or left/right keyboard
  arrows) vary that one parameter across its range.

- Two ranges give a 2D orbit: horizontal drag (or left/right keyboard
  arrows) vary one parameter while vertical drag/arrows vary the other.

At least one range is required. Supplying three ranges is an error.

For a 2D orbit, the horizontal (x) and vertical (y) axes are assigned
from whichever parameters are ranged, by priority. The x axis takes the
highest-priority ranged parameter in the order `yaw`, `pitch`, `roll`,
`light_azimuth`, `light_elevation`, and the y axis takes the other.
Camera parameters outrank light parameters, so an orbit that ranges one
of each puts the camera on horizontal drag and the light on vertical
drag. In the common case `yaw = c(0, 360), roll = c(...)` this puts yaw
on horizontal drag and roll on vertical drag;
`yaw = c(0, 360), light_elevation = c(...)` spins the camera
horizontally and raises the light vertically; and
`light_azimuth = c(0, 360), light_elevation = c(...)` moves only the
light, with azimuth horizontal and elevation vertical.

The range direction follows the order the values are written: for
example `yaw = c(360, 0)` rotates the opposite way from
`yaw = c(0, 360)`.

## Looping

When a variable axis returns to its starting view (for example a full
`yaw = c(0, 360)` turn), that axis loops seamlessly: dragging past
either end wraps around. This is detected per axis by comparing the
first and last angle modulo 360, so a full-turn axis wraps while a
partial range (such as `roll = c(-90, 90)`) clamps. `loop` can force
this on or off for all axes at once.

## Keyboard

Once the widget has focus, the arrow keys step one frame: left/right
move the horizontal axis, and (in a 2D orbit) up/down move the vertical
axis. The `r` key shows or hides the angle readout (see `readout`).

## See also

[`animate_3d()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/animate_3d.md)
for GIF/MP4 output.
[`facet_wrap_views()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/facet_wrap_views.md)
and
[`facet_grid_views()`](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/facet_wrap_views.md)
for a static figure showing several views side by side.
[orbit_3d-shiny](https://matthewkling.github.io/ggcube/reference/orbit_3d-shiny.md)
for including orbits in Shiny apps.

## Examples

``` r
# \donttest{
p <- ggplot(mountain, aes(x, y, z, fill = z, color = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(linewidth = .25) +
  coord_3d(light = light(anchor = "camera",direction = c(1, 1, 0)),
           ratio = c(1.5, 2, 1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme_void()

# 1D drag-to-rotate turntable (small n to minimize runtime)
orbit_3d(p, yaw = c(360, 0), n = 12)
#> Rendering 12 frames...
#> Assembling orbit (press `r` on the orbit to toggle its angle readout)...

# 2D orbit: drag horizontally to spin (yaw), vertically to tilt (roll)
# (note you could increase `cores` to speed up compute time)
orbit_3d(p, yaw = c(360, 0), roll = c(-90, 0), n = c(20, 10),
            width = 1000, height = 1000, cores = 1)
#> Rendering 200 frames...
#> Assembling orbit (press `r` on the orbit to toggle its angle readout)...
```
